title: A proposal for a hybrid free-space optical quantum communication network with hexagonal boron nitride-based single photon sources
authors: Julien Chénedé, Mostafa Abasifard, Tjorben Matthes, Aslı Çakan, Tobias Vogl
abstract: Hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) is known as a promising solid-state platform to host room temperature quantum emitters that produce high purity single photons. The bright and spectrally adaptable hBN emitters are space-compatible, making hBN well-suited for satellite-based free-space optical (FSO) quantum key distribution (QKD) at wavelengths where the atmospheric background is naturally suppressed. This paper presents a pathway to develop hBN emitters operating near the Ca-II Fraunhofer line (at 854 nm), enabling daylight FSO operation. Moreover, due to its compatibility with the first telecommunication window at 850 nm, it is possible to interface with optical fibers to bridge the `last mile' in a scenario where multiple end-users connect through a single optical ground station to a QKD satellite. We therefore introduce a concept that combines continuous operation of a quantum network, hybrid links to minimize deployment costs, and high data rates due to the use of realistic single photon sources. The realization would be an important milestone for the development of the quantum internet.
summary: This paper proposes a blueprint for a hybrid quantum internet by integrating satellite-based free-space quantum communication with terrestrial optical fiber networks. It leverages single-photon sources from hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) emitters operating at 854 nm, a wavelength chosen to maintain high performance during daylight hours while ensuring compatibility with existing fiber infrastructure.
main_problem: Developing a practical, hybrid free-space optical (FSO) quantum communication network capable of connecting satellites to ground stations and bridging the 'last mile' to end-users.
main_result: The paper proposes using hexagonal boron nitride (hBN) emitters operating near the Ca-II Fraunhofer line (854 nm) to achieve a balance between daylight FSO performance and compatibility with existing optical fiber infrastructure.
method: The authors developed a conceptual framework combining continuous network operation, hybrid links (space-to-ground-to-fiber), and performance modeling using realistic single-photon sources.
model_or_system: The system involves a quantum network architecture utilizing hBN-based single-photon sources for quantum key distribution (QKD) over free-space links (satellite to ground) and terrestrial fiber links.
key_observables: Secret key rate (in units of secret bit per signal), and the comparison of key rates across different wavelengths (e.g., H$\alpha$ vs. Ca-II).
important_parameters: Wavelengths (854 nm, 656 nm), link types (FSO, Fiber), and source characteristics (realistic SPS from hBN).
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that operating near Fraunhofer lines allows single photons to be separated from strong solar background radiance, and that the 854 nm wavelength balances FSO and fiber compatibility.
figures_summary: Figure 1 compares the extractable secret bit per signal for a single satellite pass at 500 km altitude, showing performance differences between daylight and nighttime conditions across various wavelengths.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the challenge of hybrid quantum networking, analyzes the performance trade-offs between different wavelengths (H$\alpha$ vs. Ca-II) for daylight operation, and proposes the 854 nm wavelength as the optimal choice for bridging space-based and fiber-based quantum links.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the engineering challenges of scaling quantum networks by proposing a concrete, multi-link architecture and identifying a practical operating wavelength that maximizes compatibility between different physical media (vacuum, air, fiber).

figures.caption: Fig. 1. The extractable secret bit per signal is shown for a single satellite (zenith) pass at an altitude of 500 km, evaluated for (a) daylight and (b) nighttime conditions. In daylight, several Fraunhofer lines, which are indicated by the labels of their corresponding elements, exhibit noticeably improved performance due to reduced background light. The ‘*’ symbols indicate the key rates achievable when using specialized Fraunhofer filters (commercially available for selected lines) that are commonly employed in solar astronomy.
